utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Hvalkof, if I could remind you of the affirmation you made yesterday which is still applicable. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Weiner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please move to tab Number 8. It's dated October 29th, 1991. So it's a letter. And could you tell us who it is to and who it's from.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's to General Strugar from Ambassador Bondioli.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Ambassador Bondioli?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the of the regional centre Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your supervisor or supervisor?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my boss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you present when this letter was drafted?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On October 29th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you present when this was drafted or did you see this letter when it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present when it was drafted, but it was given to me shortly afterwards. Of course, I can't see [phoen] the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document talks about movement of the JNA lines in violation of their agreements. Did ECMM make many protests to the JNA for violations of the movement of lines?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of in this particular case that the ECMM down in Dubrovnik had made complaints about this specific incident, and I've heard about those. But I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were any of your protests successful in having those lines moved back to their original positions?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 3 of the letter it indicates that you were going to notify or send a copy of this to the EMM -- it should be ECMM liaison officer in Belgrade. What was that. Could you tell me about that, please, or tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you were informing, of course, headquarters in Zagreb, they had copies of this. And when you send it to the liaison officer we had in Belgrade, it would normally be so that the liaison officer could communicate that to the highest authorities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you believed that -- or at least the office believed that breach of any cease-fire breaches was important enough to notify Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically because when you couldn't reach of a certain field and this one was on the 25th. And between the 25th and the 28th, the line had moved or the JNA had moved forward and apparently Mr. Bondioli was complaining about that and he wanted to make sure that some higher resources could force it through that the troops withdrew to the line they were at the 25th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could you move to tab Number 23, please. We're at tab 23. In the middle of the document it says: November 28th, in the middle of the first page. Is that date correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. I have given remarks about that before. It for sure -- it should be -- read October 28th, because that was the day, as I also mentioned yesterday, the radio centre became operative. And Mr. Bondioli was working very hard and was very busy, so it's an error he made that day. And he made it also further down the page. And I have given remarks about that before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you first tell us what type of document this is.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- let's say -- I would call an assessment of the situation and a sort of a report from Mr. Bondioli to the head of the ECMM mission, Ambassador Fernhaufen [phoen] in Zagreb where he sort of gives his first impressions of what is happening in the area of responsibility he has just taken control over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you just look at the last page for a moment, and based on reading the last page could you give us an idea of -- although you said it mentions October 28th or it should refer to October 28th on the first page, when this document was prepared by looking at the last page.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is obvious because now we are talking about -- it's obvious it's made before the 29th of November, because now he is mentioning this in the week up to the 10th of November, and he wouldn't write anything like that. And it is true. It is -- it was made -- I can't give you the exact date, but it was made, I believe, about the 1st of November, maybe the last date of -- yeah, or maybe the last date of October. But I can't remember exactly the day he wrote it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the second page.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a date on the second line.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, November 2nd -- yeah, well -- sorry. I said 1st. Anyway, it was written before the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the second, the first full paragraph on the second page, which is kind of in the middle, it starts HRC --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you say that from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first full paragraph on page 2, it starts HRC and previously paid a courtesy call.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look to the fourth line down it says: "The EC declaration on Dubrovnik of November 27th," what date should that read?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It again should be October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it said: "Was delivered to General Strugar, commander of the 2nd MD." What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd MD should be the 2nd military district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that located? Can you read that in --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to my information, that was the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says: "In" -- can you read MIL -- is that Miljine [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Miljine, which is down in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says: "In that of -- on -- that of November 28th. Is that date correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Yugoslavia to General Vukovic in Zitnic. Was Zitnic within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. That's up in the area -- Krajina area. It's a little bit north -- well, a little bit north of Sebra [phoen] -- of the Zadar, up in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this letter maintained in the files at the regional centre in Split?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were sending nearly daily negotiating with General Vukovic and his representatives from Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go to the third page, please. Now, if we go down to the 11th line, it says in the middle: "Assurances about keeping the cease-fire were repeatedly provided by the two generals to the RCS teams."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two generals mentioned above on that page are both Strugar and Vukovic. Did they abide by these assurances to maintain the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two generals that made these assurances, who are they?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vukovic and General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. Sir, I'd like to move back to where we started towards the beginning to a group of documents which all concern the month of November, documents 9, 10, 11, and 12, concerning November 9th.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say again, 9th --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They relate to November 9th. They're documents 9, 10, 11, and 12. We'll take them as a group but one by one, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could start with document -- tab Number 9. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how this information was received.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was received on the SatCom from our ECMM team in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what seems to be the problem that's happening in this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's that shelling is going on continuously in the area. It had increased, and both -- you can read and I can easily remember that, that targets were closing in and now they mentioned the detailed places on Lokrum island where it's pronounced, ready, Lapad and Svei Jakov and fires crossing the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that first page in number 3 you wrote: "We appeal to HRC Split, now in Zagreb, that he sends an urgent message to JNA General Strugar and headquarters in Belgrade asking them to order immediate cease of fire over Dubrovnik." First: What do you mean by: "HRC Split now in Zagreb"?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Bondioli was in Zagreb for consultations with the head of the ECM mission, so I was his acting representative in Split at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was a request being made to contact General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about, I understand, why the ECMM monitors in Dubrovnik are asking this question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they felt very much under pressure and they had not for a long time had a pleasant time in Dubrovnik, so they wanted help from the highest authorities, which I do understand very well and I did understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are referring to General Strugar because he was the commander of the forces opposing Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar ever advise the ECMM that he was not the commander of the JNA forces in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I've never heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar ever tell the ECMM that he lacked authority to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar ever tell the ECMM that their requests or protests were being made to the wrong person?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar ever advise the ECMM that they should send their requests to someone else?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we continue on this document, if we could move to page 3. Could you tell us about this document.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the top says who signed it. They were three ECMM members who were on the team in Dubrovnik, an Italian diplomat, a Greek colonel, and a Czechoslovakian, that time a Czechoslovakian colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page. "Reasons to evacuate ECMM mission from Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does a monitoring team has to provide reasons for evacuation? Is evacuation considered serious? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they sit down there and they were feeling very miserable and I was actually feeling miserable having unarmed men sitting as neutral peacekeepers in the middle of a shelling show, you're not sending people, monitors or military observers out to get killed. So I felt and I -- we felt responsible for these people. At the same time, it was sort of -- they were informed they had to tell themselves when they wanted to get out. And now they had reached the point they are giving reasons why they want to be moved out of the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you agree with their basis for evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move to the next document, Document Number 10, please. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote it myself or anyway, I signed it. Maybe somebody else helped me to write it, but I certainly know what is there and I had made the -- expressed what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that document is dated November 9th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the same date as the previous document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who did you send the letter to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's your signature on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. And what is the basis of this letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the selling of -- the ongoing shelling down there, protesting about that, reference to the message we just had been talking about from the militaries down in Dubrovnik. So I'm thinking in a reasonably kind way asking to have the nonsense stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the second paragraph you talk about the security of the monitors.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says that they could not leave. Why couldn't the monitors leave at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dubrovnik was surrounded from the land side and there was a naval blockade by the JN -- or the Yugoslavian navy, so you could not stay in Dubrovnik. So it was impossible to leave Dubrovnik in a safe way if you did not have, let's say, that was a fact anyway, permission from the JNA forces, that meant from the command, in my opinion from General Strugar, to be sure that there was cease of fire so these people could get out, and permission, as we could not go by land, permission to send some vessel, rowing boat or whatever, to Dubrovnik to get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I ask you to look at the next document, also dated November 9th. And is that your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when I say "the next document," I'm referring to the document at tab 11.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you send this to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent this to the JNA in Split, which means to General Mladenic who was strange for me. He was a major general of a naval base. He was the -- what I would call and we would call in peacekeeping language, the local authority in Split. We communicated with daily and when we had no chance, which we often had difficulties of passing information to other JNA forces, for example, in the Dubrovnik area we would pass it through the naval headquarters in Split to be sure that it came out. Because it was our understanding that the communication between the Yugoslavian forces was quite good and went well, whereas we had -- within our organisations in the fast way it was built-up, we had problems with communications. So we informed also Split this way about the local authorities in Split about the situation and hoped that that could help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where was the Split base located in relation to your offices? Was it far away? Was it a short distance?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of kilometres. As far as I remember it was called Lora base. It was quite a big establishment. And that was where it was an enclave of -- like you have many places in the Croatian territory, an enclave of the JNA units surrounded by Croatia and whatever there was of small Croatian units. There was another barrack in Split which we actually later on evacuated down to the Lora base before the whole lot was evacuated out of Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the first sentence, sir, it says, sentence number 1: "I prefer to my protest earlier today." Who protest are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the one we've just talked of -- what was that? Number 10. Yeah. And as I have to recall it today - it is a long time ago - but we sent a copy of the other one also. It was either handed over to a liaison officer or it was sent down to Lora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "number 10," are you referring to tab 10, the protest to general --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your tab 10, yeah. And I can add to that. I might also or one of my staff officers might also have done that extra-verbally on the local -- one of the local daily meetings we normally had with the representatives of the JNA. And they either took place in the morning up in our headquarters or they took place at the Lora base or at a hotel I've forgotten the name of down in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could we move to the final document concerning that date, number 12, tab Number 12, please. Could you look at it and tell us if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's not a pleasant look. The handwriting was absolutely horrible. I was very busy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my handwriting. And I'm very sorry to admit it, but it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is this?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, lots of things happened and I was called to the communications room where I had a very excellent team of French non-commissioned officers. And they said, there's something important; they want to talk to you personally. It happened now and then. And then I got this actually from a Dane. And it tells in Danish, we are down on the floor. Well, that's quite clever in a situation like this. The hotel has been hit. There's an impact on the hotel close to a window. The JNA is shelling Orsula or shooting at Orsula from canon belts. And now I have really problems reading my own handwriting; I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It and -- the eastern approach to Dubrovnik -- distance to the hotel, approximately 1 to 1 and a half kilometres. The island Lokrum is under heavy shelling or fire all morning. One missile. Machine gun fire close to the hotel. Helicopter in the area at most likely an artillery observer -- observation helicopter. At 11.55, a recce plane was crossing. The plane was of the type M-4 Bison. And then I've just written here the report was -- is sent via Zagreb to Belgrade or this. During that day all -- well, every information coming in of that nature was passed on to Zagreb and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you got this from a Danish associate. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fellow was a Danish airforce officer, who was belonging to the ECMM team in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the second page --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: And may I -- sorry. May I add that he was not the leader of the team, because he was ordered to pass the message by the leader of the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to the second page. Now, on the second page it says: "JNA General Strugar" -- number 3 it says: "We appeal to HQ -- or headquarters, RC Split now in Zagreb that he sends a message urgently to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. General Strugar in -- headquarters in Belgrade." Is that the reference in earlier tab 9 letter that we referred to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It it's -- it's the same request. To be honest right now, I don't know if the second time we got it, but it's the same request from the same people, yes. It might have been passed twice; that I cannot recall today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go to page 5, please. There's a note. It says: "1520," which is 3 hours and 20 minutes in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm -- now I'm not aware of what you're talking about. Would you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's an ERN number or number on the top right. 02187325.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, here. Now I'm there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's a column and it says 1520 or we would say 3.20 in the afternoon. Could you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm in doubt of the first word, but it looks like it says: "Witnesses the shelling of the Old City. At least two shells landed on the church in the city, bursting great amount of smoke." Then I can't read what is the next, but it says: "Close to Domino church."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what do they say at 1505 hours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several attempts to JNA headquarters." That means several attempts to get in contact with JNA headquarters, and they are mentioning that the attempts were not successful because the general in the JNA headquarters was busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could we go two more pages down to the page which has the numbers at the top, 7327, the last four digits. And it says something about crisis committee to JNA.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an answer from the crisis committee to the JNA on an ultimatum they received earlier from General Strugar concerning a ceasefire which he proposed to come into effect at 1430 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what does it say under that? Can you read that, read that please, where we --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We received this answer at 1445 hours local time. The answer is: Your ultimatum demands us to accept your proposal for a demarcation line. In the first place we point out that our forces have not once violated the cease-fire and that they answer only when forced to prevent your attacks. We cannot accept your proposal for the demarcation line for the many reasons explained several times at the negotiations in Saftat. Our proposal for the demarcation line is fair enough. Collected to our damage regarding the lines occupied by both sides at the time of the agreed cease-fire on October 25th, 1991, at 1700 hours. So we ask you to study it carefully in order to be able to discuss it at the negotiations scheduled for 10 November 1991 at 1100 hours in Saftat. We take the obligation of not firing first, except when forced to reject your attack. Signed by the President of the crisis committee Zeljko Zigic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, was this document maintained in your records at the regional centre in Split?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. As you can see, it's again my nasty handwriting, so it's one I had been on the SatCom to receive from the ECMM in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you usually receive messages, whether it's fax or through communications, from the crisis committee or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Crisis Staff or the crisis committee, as they called themselves, normally communicated their messages straight to the EC monitors in Dubrovnik, and then they forwarded them to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It also happened that they passed it if they had possibilities, both to the monitors in Dubrovnik and directly to us, if there was a possibility. It was varied a bit, but we had information generally often and from a routine from them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what this crisis committee was, this crisis committee in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it reminded me about my childhood during the war. And as a group we had something called the liberty council. It seemed to be a group of intellectuals, idealists, maybe nationalists, anyway of people who had the respect of the population in Dubrovnik who had sort of more or less -- maybe both selected but also elected themselves as leaders and were respected as such. I'm not sure that this was right, but this was my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people involved in negotiations, cease-fire negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the -- in some places, I believe they were. I have no records in general of who took part on the Croatian side in the meetings with the JNA. I have no record of it, and I didn't take part in it before I came down on November -- or December the 5th. But at that time, I believe they were crisis committee member people. And now and then I will have to add, it could be difficult to distinguish for me or maybe there was not even a difference, because you had -- we were receiving information from the crisis committee. We were receiving information directly, as you will note some places, from the mayor of Dubrovnik. But there was no doubt that they worked together and later on when I met them, they were together, whatever they were, crisis committee or the mayor's office, it seemed to be the closely-connected group, respected by the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could we move on to the next four documents which would be tabs 13 through 16, relating to November 10th.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. What did you say? The 14th --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 13. 13 through 16. We'll take those four documents together, relating to November 10th. Could you look at document number 13 first. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was written on my orders and in connection with me by one of my staff officers and signed by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us, what is the -- just summarise the letter, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I add this, that this is still many years ago and there are lots of paper, and I remember that yesterday somebody was questioning why I didn't know all this by heart or what have you. Well, maybe it's because of my old age, but it is difficult to remember all this, so I will have to have a look at it. And anyway, I know what I wrote, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could look at it for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It says on the top: "Protest from headquarters of regional centre, European monitoring mission, Split, to General Mladenic JNA naval headquarters, Split." Why were you sending a letter to Split first?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we had difficulties getting in contact the other way down to Dubrovnik. As I mentioned before, when we had problems that way, we would try to go through General Mladenic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 1, the last two lines it says: "I strongly protest against this continued serious breach of the cease-fire and through you request that it be restored." Was shelling continuing in that -- on that date, on the 10th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to take any action to have it cease on that date?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did our best. I know the monitors down in Dubrovnik did their best to get in contact and pass information with no success. And while this was one of the ways we did -- we tried to do it from the Split end. And we also -- well, I don't have all these files from the headquarters in Split or our regional headquarters, but we passed, as I have mentioned before, in normal good military way, all information to our headquarters in Zagreb. And I cannot say what they did up there, but I'm absolutely sure that they did their very best from their end to pass the information to the proper side on the Yugoslav part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we turn to the next tab, tab 14, also dated November 10th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could we go to the letter on the second page. Now, is that your signature on the bottom of the letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you look at it for a moment, become familiar with it again, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that letter is from the EC monitoring team in Split to General Strugar, admiral Jokic and Admiral Letica. Why were you sending the letter to the three individuals, beginning with Strugar?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Strugar was, as mentioned several times before, according to us, the whole of our knowledge, the commander of the JNA forces surrounding Dubrovnik. This letter is concerning also a movement on ship. And as we were then -- I'm an army person but dealing with the navy, I thought it would be proper to approach the admiral in the area, and we knew Admiral Jokic was on down in that area and attached to the best of our knowledge to General Strugar. So that would be a decent way of addressing it to him, too. And that, now, letter, sir, is -- again this confusing thing from us. He was a Croat admiral, apparently retired, I think, earlier from the Yugoslavian navy, but now he was the commander of the Croat forces in the Split area. And when we want to move around and anyway it's a question of opposing parties, and we want to move around safely, it's appropriate to inform both sides what we are doing, what we intend to do. And I can add that all this -- this was also sent through Zagreb. It was reported -- they got this and they were asked and I don't have any documents of that, to approach the highest authorities in Belgrade and what have you to have the message passed down through those lines. And we actually succeeded -- I don't have those papers, but we got it in -- on fax messages, a confirmation from Zagreb that our plan -- it was slightly changed later, but the general plan lined up here was accepted by Belgrade, that means by the -- to the best of my knowledge, by minister of defence or whatever, title he might have, the equivalent, in Belgrade, which meant that information should have been passed down to General Strugar or the other people responsible for the Dubrovnik area. And the same information was passed then to Croatian forces in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to the next tab, Number 15, also dated November 10th. Could you look at it for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you're familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it before, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's to General Kadijevic minister of defence from, and it's signed from head of mission, DJ Van Houten. Who was Mr. Van Houten?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Van Houten was a Dutch ambassador and head of the ECMM, that meant he was the commander in my war language for the ECMM sitting at the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for sending this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to ask the ambassador, but I -- of course I am -- I don't doubt what was the reason he wanted to support and help people under his command. And he wanted, of course, a cease-fire down in the area. But he was concerned about the monitors' lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the third sentence, which begins in the middle of line four it says: "This breach of the cease-fire has been brought to the attention of General Raseta, deputy commander of 5 military district, and General Strugar, commander of the forces in Dubrovnik area, without any response." Had you received any response as of that date, which is the 10th, to your statements or protests to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that something you would have notified Zagreb, the lack of response?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could we move to the final letter of that date.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 16.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you look at it for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what type of message this is. Is it a letter or a message or a fax? What is it basically?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a -- you could call it a message passed from Dubrovnik and coming through the ops room, that means the operations room, from the monitors -- had down in Dubrovnik. So they had received this in writing from President Zeljko Zigic. We had had his name up before. And then they are passing this on the SatCom, which has been working still at this stage. And it's noted down by one of my staff officers or one from my communications section, and passed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it says on the top to the left: "Republic of Croatia, assembly of Dubrovnik," and it's signed President Zeljko Zigic." What is the assembly of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the organisation of how -- I'm not familiar with it. As I mentioned before, it could be a bit confusing. But the way I understand it is that that is what I would call the town council. But -- and anyway, this man was well-known to the monitors and I met him later on myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you file and maintain files of letters that you received from the local assembly or local crisis committee?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We filed all appropriate material, as I mentioned yesterday, and we forwarded whatever -- and we would forward, for example, for us something like this to our headquarters in Zagreb. And by the way, if you want to know how we forwarded it, we had a secure fax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Zagreb, not anywhere else, but to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could we move to a document which is tab 24, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tab 24, Your Honours. It's a long document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is dated the next day, November 11th. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's unfortunately again my handwriting in a busy time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we look at this document, could you tell us what is happening now, beginning November 11th.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this time, as we had requested and that we could go down to Dubrovnik to pick up the monitors. But we had also got permission and agreed by both sides and confirmed through our headquarters in Zagreb that we could bring back wounded people, old people, children, pregnant women, and women in general, and in case we had place for nationals out of Dubrovnik, and we could bring down, if we had the possibility, of water, potatoes, gas, fuel, and that was essential to us, because it was not anywhere nice to just go down and take out our own people when you were surrounded by people in a miserable situation. So we wanted to help as many people as we could. We had got this information or we had got the approval. So then we had it organised that we could go by ship, and it was also approved that we could move out of Split harbour and that was approved by the Yugoslavian navy. So we left Split, and as you can see at 1650 we actually had permission. That means permission granted by the Yugoslavian navy that we could leave on this ferry, Partizanska, to move not to move to Dubrovnik but to the isle of Hvar [Realtime transcript read in error "Wa"]. At the isle of Hvar we had -- and we had found out and there was this old Danish ferry, Slavija, and it was loaded with supplies, essential supplies for Dubrovnik, but because of a blockade, a naval blockade, it had not been able to move further, so we stopped at Hvar which is a place I'm not -- frankly, normally had never stopped at. So we had arranged that was a ship we could move down with. I can add at this stage also that we had been informed and fully accepted that and understood why that when we are moving down here to Dubrovnik, we could not go straight to Dubrovnik, but we had to go to Zelenika [Realtime transcript read in error "Selenika"] so that the JNA could inspect the ships to prove that we were not bringing ammunition, guns, rockets, and loads of soldiers down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was fair enough, and we had this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, "Wa" should be Hvar, and "Zelenika" is Z-e-l-e-n-i-k-a.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say "we got permission," and "we're doing this," who is doing this?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The we, that is the "we" as the representatives of ECMM and "we," the representatives present in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who led the group?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, according to the notes here you arrive in Zelenika on November 12th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with anyone from the JNA on that date?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was difficult to get into Zelenika. The captain was called and we were stopped outside the harbour as mentioned at 6.55 on the 12th of November. And we were told we -- they were not informed we were coming; they didn't want us to enter the harbour. Because I could not understand what was going on, so it was the captain of the ship who had the conversation on the ship's radio. I talked to him and asked him to inform about the agreement as I was informed, that we were expected. It was all accepted. Anyway, finally we were permitted to enter and we harboured at 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet anyone from the JNA once you arrived in Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we stopped or whatever -- I'm used to -- I'm not a navy man. But as soon as the ship was harboured, it was my -- in my language, I don't know what it is in English, a "leider", a sort of a ladder down the side of the boat. And up came a small navy officer. He was already talking while he was climbing up and he was not in a good mood. Even before he really presented himself, he was talking about a criminal ship and criminal people and illegal arrival and not being informed. Anyway, we found out that this man was a commander, a captain, Kapitan, whatever, Jeremic. That's the name we got the other thing I think I had spelled out somehow. Anyway, he called him Jeremic. And he was specifically referring to -- the good ship Slavija had taken part in the earlier peace convoy, which -- where President Stipe Mesic was along, lots of boats going down earlier. And he said, as he had taken part in that, that convoy had brought down military equipment or troops or God knows what. So the ship was criminal. It was the first criminal ship actually I met. But the crew was criminal, too. And they had to be arrested. And besides that, nobody was aware that we were coming and what was I doing there, et cetera. He was not, I would say, a kind man. He was a very upset and arrogant little man. Well, I've never been scared of people, so actually I said -- well, I said: You should be informed about this. You should have been aware. And I had, which I don't have anymore, I had a sort of a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fax, a confirmation, from Zagreb telling that the trip had been approved. So I said: You will have to notify your superior about this, and I want to talk as soon as possible to these people. And I also demanded that I had got -- had means of communication. So I wanted to -- I said: I want a place where I -- there is a telephone and a fax machine. And I would like to give that navy officer credit, because suddenly he changed and became a very polite and nice man and within no time we had an office -- occupied an office in the harbour area, not too far from the ship, and with a fax machine and a phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you a few questions and then we'll get back to that. On your first page, on November 12th, it says: "At 10.00, General Strugar denies Slavija to enter Dubrovnik. Only ECMM monitors can get consent." Can you tell me what that's about.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well as I said, we got into this office. And then I tried to pass messages to people I thought it was necessary to pass messages to. And one of the messages was of course, as I'd said before to this navy officer, that there was an agreement that we could come, that they could check the ship, and then that we could proceed to Dubrovnik. And I wanted him to remind his superiors, that was General Strugar, about this. This was done on some -- apparently on the telephone there. I can't really -- it must have been on that phone or whatever. And the answer was that General Strugar denies Slavija to enter Dubrovnik. Only EC monitors can get out, and that meant get out of Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to page 7 which has the last -- on the top the number 0218, but the last four numbers, 7304. And you have notes in two conversations. A conversation on the top, there's a blank space in the middle, and then a conversation on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That refers -- that note refers to the conversation I had with Captain Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, being your notes, can you read that first paragraph, the conversation of what he said.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On behalf of General Strugar, the above-mentioned gentleman declared that we could not go into Dubrovnik because Mr. Stipe Mesic" - may be spelling this wrong - "had misused the convoy to bring in armed CNG personnel. He knew that because they had taken some of these very persons as POWs, thus the confidence in Croatians and EC monitors had suffered severely. Slavija could not go to Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does this concern that earlier conversation you had with General -- I'm sorry, with Captain Sofronije that day --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry, Sofronije, Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And down below there's a second paragraph and it says -- looks like 10.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 10.00 in the morning. And could you read that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The ship cannot go to Dubrovnik. The members of the EC mission can. The EC team from Dubrovnik can also leave. These people on the PC caused about ten casualties. PC is the peace convoy. There is no cease-fire yet because they are shooting at us all the time. General Strugar suggests that we go to Cavtat by car and then with a boat to the Old City or the ship Argus will bring us, will bring the monitors out of Dubrovnik and bring them to Zelenika." And then I don't know what I meant with no cars; I can't say. But this is what I had been writing down at the time receiving this information by Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this conversation, is this the one that you referred to as 10.00 a.m. On November 12th, on the first page --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's continuing -- there was a long conversation with that captain that morning, but this is at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you -- since this is a telephone conversation, did this occur in that office that you were telling us about?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was -- there was no communications to land at, let's say, in general from the ship except the ship's radio. And we had to go down. That's why I wanted communications, obviously. So we went down, found that office. He found that for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what did you do in that office? Tell the Court what you were doing that morning.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking, trying to persuade -- on our behalf trying to persuade now in this case Captain Jeremic to bring on to his superiors that we had to do -- we had go, trying to get in contact, and report to Belgrade -- or sorry, to Zagreb through the various channels we might have or where we could get telephone contact or fax contact about our situation, what we were doing, like sending back a normal SITREP as you normally do when you are out on a job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 2 on this document. Towards the middle of the page it says -- at 10.45, it says: "Contact with German embassy in order to relay the latest message from General Strugar through him." What's the contact with embassies about or what is that all about?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you know, as I've said before, now and then communication difficult. I don't know why. I thought the telephone system was supposed to work properly in Yugoslavia -- normally it was. But we could not get through. It is part of my duty to report to my headquarters. And then I had numbers of the various embassies in Belgrade, and they were members of the EC. And that was a possibility of passing proper information. And I knew the various embassies would help me, the EC embassies, would help me. So that was a way of passing information to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the next time note at 11.20, it says: "I informed Belgrade about General Strugar's latest proposals and my reports." And then Mr. Cunningham informed me --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then my replies, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the latest report or proposals and your reply, your reports?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- what I was trying to get through at that time was the denial of movement out of Zelenika going to Dubrovnik. It took time. It takes time. And specifically in a situation like this. I was trying to pass this message. General Strugar does not want us to go, as we were promised, to go to Dubrovnik. He wants to keep us here or he would only let the monitors out. And also at the same time, that's what I wanted to pass and that's actually what I passed. I said -- I can add here now, I said: I am not and the monitors are not leaving Zelenika before it is back where it came from. And I felt -- we felt responsible for the crew the ship. And we were actually in our presence verbally threatened by Captain Jeremic. We were told they were criminals and they were -- they ought to be arrested. So then, said we better stay and they have to arrest us, too, if they want to arrest people with a diplomatic passport. We had to use that later on. We didn't show them a diplomatic passport at the time. They ought to be aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you told them: I am not -- excuse me -- that you were not leaving Zelenika before it is back where it came from. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the fact that when they wanted -- didn't want to release the ship, and this was a criminal ship, then -- well, I was sort of responsible that it came back. I -- we had arranged it; we got approval. They went down with us because they trusted us and the neutrality of the ship when we were on board. The ship was not bringing any war materiel, soldiers, or anything, except us and the goodies and a few truck drivers and some other people, civilians, who were no danger to anybody, and realised that apparently by the JNA, too. So I mean that I wanted to be sure -- I felt responsible for this, that we followed this ship to the bitter end, whatever the end had to be. It had to be, in my opinion, out and back to Croatian territory where it came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any attempt to contact General Strugar on that date?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried. I asked to have a meeting with him. And that was again through Jeremic or, I think -- I can't remember that exactly, but after we got communication if Jeremic left later on. But then we had the telephone. And one of my men was a German diplomat who spoke Serbian or Croatian or both and -- very well, and maybe he is the one who has passed it. But I have asked several times that we had a meeting. We've also told that the general was busy - generals very often are - and somebody else would arrive and talk to us. And this gentleman showed up about 1500 hours in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at your document it says right around 12.40 -- 12.42: "General Strugar's two IC to be here in two hours." What does the two IC mean?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means second in command; that was what we were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any other means of communication on that date, other than the room?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we had sort of ended up with no results and we found out we couldn't move and what have you, anyway we were stuck because we were not allowed to leave. Then I didn't intend to sit in that lousy office the rest of the day, so I wanted to go back to the ship. So I demanded in a polite way to have a telephone brought on board to my cabin in the ship. And this was kindly arranged fast and efficient and highly appreciated. So thank you to the JNA for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next page. If we go to the next page, at 1.05 there's a message from Bondioli and there's a message down to Strugar. "Agreement from yesterday is still in effect at 1305 or 1.05 in the afternoon." What's that about, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well as you know, Ambassador Bondioli was not in Split, I think I mentioned that before, when I left the place. And then now he's suddenly back. And he wants to assist and help. So he's -- we managed to get a message from him through this telephone that all cargo except Red Cross, but including these will be left in Zelenika. Well, a cease-fire would be effective from time of Slavija's departure from Zelenika and the Dutch foreign minister wants direct talks with General Strugar. Well, what he is -- he was aware of the situation, but actually the -- what we had on board was relief for the people of Dubrovnik, as I said, water, potatoes, and gas bottles, because there was no way to get hot food there. And so he has been talking to people, apparently -- I don't know, in Zelenika -- in Split, and then he sent this message. And then he also passes a message that the Dutch foreign minister would like to talk to General Strugar. And then I put a note here, I need a telephone number, to General Strugar -- no, sorry, to the Dutch foreign minister, and to General Strugar of course, and I passed this straight to the JNA liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to the next day, the 13th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were on tab 17, your hand notes. And I'd ask you to go to page 9, which has the ERN number of 0218, with the last three digits of 306. So it should be 7306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean to say tab 17? I suspect you mean tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tab 24, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 24, page 9. Do you have -- at 11.45, General Strugar talked to the captain, but only said something like: We finished the whole thing, then banged the phone, telephone. Could you tell us what that's about, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apparently -- I can't remember exactly how it came in, but the captain and General Strugar had a contact. And the only information I got out of the captain was this, which I have quoted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is on November 13th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I cannot -- could not understand the language, then it's -- it appeared to me to be a conversation about the criminal ship and whatever goodies we were bringing on board that ship and the departure of the ship, et cetera. But that's what I know about that conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that everything was finished, were you allowed to leave on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not leaving on the 13th -- wait a minute. Now I -- I have to go back here. Yeah, we were leaving -- sorry, we were leaving on the 13th. Yes, we were leaving on the 13th. We came down on the 12th; we were leaving on the 13th around noon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it says at that same page of 1305, 1.05 p.m., Slavija left Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we go to the next document, which is document at tab 17, also dated November 13th.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no document at tab 13 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. 17, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at that and familiarise yourself with that, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this time, apparently there has been proper information given from various contacts at higher levels. So Ambassador Bondioli, the head of the regional centre Split sends a message to General Strugar and the crisis committee in Dubrovnik of course, because both sides had to be informed. So he requests for them to confirm an effective cease-fire will be in force. So the good ship Slavija can move safely to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it says -- there was some notes on there. It says: "Received at 12.35," and it says: "Not possible to" -- could you tell us what those markings mean that are at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the marking that I received this at 12.35, and the other one -- and part of it has disappeared. To the best of my -- what I remember, it means it was not possible for me to get in contact with anybody at the time. So I couldn't sort of reply to this or give any answer to it. Anyway, I can also remember that I was quite satisfied. I hoped that that was okay. And shortly afterwards it was confirmed, as far as I remember. And then we could leave and we left. But a long discussion as you might see from the notes, and lots of problems had to be dealt with during the evening and the night and the morning before this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you go to tab 19 now. Now, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. This was written by my German colleague, Mr. Haupt who I mentioned before who spoke the local language. And he was along with me when we had any talks with people from the JNA or the captain or anybody who spoke Yugoslavian language. And this is written in connection with the meeting we had of this person we talked and anyway were told on the phone would be the two IC of General Strugar. Colonel Damjanovic, Radomir, that was what we were informed was his rank and his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it has a conversation. It says: "Hvalkof"?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is because he was taking notes, so he was noting apparently what I said, or not apparently. He was noting down what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the third line it says -- on the fourth line: "We should go with Slavija to Dubrovnik. Any alternative would be less desirable."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was my point of view that we had to carry out this expedition as planned and agreed upon. And I saw no reason whatsoever why we should change our mind. And in particular, in respect of the crew we had on board and in respect of the sort of promise which Dubrovnik crisis committee was also informed about that we could take out not only the monitors but take out people who really needed to be taken out of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the next line it says: "General Strugar could solve this problem."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my opinion. It would be -- the way I was thinking, the way I'm still thinking, is the only one who could give us permission to leave could make the decision would be the commander of the JNA in the local area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the second page is a letter from Bondioli. Could you tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, of course I saw this -- I can't remember when I saw -- probably got it the same day. I can't remember exactly. But I know this letter, and of course this is an appreciation from Ambassador Bondioli that we actually succeeded in arriving. And there was a cease-fire, so we could get into Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's -- on page, I'm sorry. On tab 18 we find the same document as the second page of tab 19.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my own note of it. So I probably received it twice. This has been the first thing. The details I cannot remember, but I certainly wrote it down and I even passed -- noted the time, 11.25, yeah. So it -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to send this note from ECMM to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I at the time -- no. I -- we were on board the ship waiting to leave, but I assumed that Mr. Bondioli has either the pass originally to both the JNA headquarters, to the crisis committee in Dubrovnik, and to me that they have tried to pass it through by other means, but I cannot prove that it ended up where it was supposed to. I know now that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the last document on this matter, Document Number 20. A very difficult one to read -- tab 20, please. It's to Mr. Bondioli from the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I have seen it before, but I find it very, very difficult to read now. And I found it very difficult, I recall, to read it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person whose name is on the bottom is?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I read -- actually the B/C/S copy is easier to read. But if I can read just the first two lines. It says: "Our promises fulfilled. Ferry Slavija sent off to Dubrovnik." And the next line is: "Fire cease." What is that about the cease-fire and the ferry leaving?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is all what we had fought for and asked for. What we ended up with sort of having an approval, that they would cease fire, they would not be shelling us or, most important, not Dubrovnik so we could enter peacefully. And that is what it tells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next section of the letter it talks about a meeting to take Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. place on November 14th. Did a meeting in fact take place on November 14th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A meeting took place, but not a Cavtat, for various reasons. Because the crisis committee, when I met them in Dubrovnik wanted me to go down to Cavtat. But because of my experiences in Zelenika and the whole situation, I denied, regretfully, to go. I said, I will not leave the ship Slavija before we are back where we came from. But I succeeded later on -- actually in the morning of the 14th, to have -- I think that was from the ship's radio and the crisis committee who had contact with the JNA, I succeeded in having arranged a meeting with three members of the crisis committee in Zelenika on the 14th. And I got it approved from all sides that these members of the crisis committee could go down back to Zelenika where we now had to be inspected and promised to be inspected again by the JNA, so they could see that we were not bringing out criminals or people who were fighting people or whatever. So that was a promise. So we had to go back to Zelenika to be inspected again. Then I found it would be quite good if we could bring the crisis committee members down for a negotiation in Zelenika, as they wanted to negotiate further cease-fire problems. That was accepted. But we also had to promise to give-and-take every time, anyway the way I was brought up when you discussed this sort of thing, to give-and-take. So we had to, of course, accept some of the JNA ideas and wishes, and that was the ship Slavija should not ever again -- or we should not on that ship enter Dubrovnik again. So then we had to make an arrangement so a pilot boat or some other vessel could come out in the open sea and pick up the three members of the crisis committee when we returned after having been Zelenika and when we were proceeding north, at that time, planned for Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we move to tab 21, which are some notes concerning that meeting of November 14th.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, tab 21?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, because that is from the meeting in Zelenika we were just talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these your notes or someone else's?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Mr. Haupt's notes. He was my colleague, and he was the interpreter. He was a German diplomat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Mr. Haupt and I and the other people who I mentioned above, two navy officers, one which I knew, or who I knew, Captain Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you turn to page 3 on your evaluation. If you look at the first part on JNA, it says: "Makes clear that involvement of ECMM is tolerated but not desired." What's the basis of that statement?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is that it was sort of actually said very clear that they didn't like our presence, but we were tolerated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you have access to all the areas controlled by the Croats? When I say "you," did the ECMM monitors have access to all of those areas?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had problems going anywhere on the Croatian side, that is so, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the areas controlled by the JNA? Did the ECM monitors have free access to those areas?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that it has not happened that ECMM monitors have been moving a bit around, but to the best of my knowledge, not. And in general, no, we were not wanted to move around. And, for example, this is where I have been in JNA area before that time, it has been up in the Knin area, while we was under heavy escort up to Knin, and no move around, discussion, maybe sleeping up there, no chance of moving out of the place, and I never really wished to, and then back again. No moving around. We did not know like observers in a mission like that. Normally we did not experience freedom of movement on that side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that you did not have free access to the JNA areas, or JNA-controlled areas, what effect did that have on your abilities, the monitors' abilities to function?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my way of thinking, it made life much more difficult and much more difficult to carry out the task we had. From all the other places I'd been, we might not have been wanted but we were also always accepted. And we had freedom of movement. And when you are on both sides in a conflict, when neutral people, you have a much better chance, as I mentioned earlier, to get in contact and to get to know each other and to solve problems before they escalate and end up in insane situations. We had no really chance to interfere and drop in and talk to senior officers when the situation was becoming serious on the JNA side. It had to be this conference where we always had to meet, again if we wanted meetings, on the JNA side and then go back again. That meant when that we were -- well, we had no -- if something happened, we had no way of doing something here and now, possibility on that side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that affect your relationships between the side that didn't give you free access?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were sorry about it and you can also say annoyed about it. We only had the power of words and no force. We had to work on the good will of both sides. So of course it had an effect, yes, on our way of that we could not -- we felt that we could not do the job as we wanted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move to tab 22, please. Do you know what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is an Italian monitor, Mr. Ghidi's report to Mr. Bondioli -- well, we had a normal report from the team he belonged to. But he was an Italian and Mr. Bondioli wanted a report from him personally, which was very good. I think Mr. Ghidi was a very good and excellent monitor, very serious and not scared of his life. He might be, but he didn't behave like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this diary or log from the monitoring team, when is it prepared? Is it prepared while they're there? They prepare notes each day, or is it prepared upon completion? Or could you tell us how it's drafted.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ghidi did like any monitor, to the best of my knowledge, take notes when he was out on the job. And then he was asked to make this report to Mr. Bondioli. So he was sitting down on the 18th of November in Split and taking out his notes and make this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive daily information from these monitors, other than this information contained in this report?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received daily information. We normally had twice a day what you could call a radio schedule where they gave reports of the situation, what had happened, up to that time from Dubrovnik and from other -- the other places, Zadar, Sibenik. And whenever something important happened, they would report immediately to our communications' group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you turn to page 6 of that report, please, which concerns November 10th and 11th.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the one numbered 7266?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you. Now, it talks about heavy shelling as never seen continued by land, Zarnovica, and sea, four ships. And then a little later it says at least five anti-tank rockets against the Old City walls and the old port, going into the next page. Some shelling, as reported touched the old inner city. We could not witness the damages, not being able to leave the hotel. Did you receive that type of information through the communications system?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you be able to say whether this report is consistent with the daily messages you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this report filed?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this information also forwarded to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry. I'm sure it was, but I can't sit here and confirm it. I'm sure it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you filed reports like this --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- within your system in Split?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move now to tab Number 25, a document dated November 20th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Would you look at the letter, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this letter before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Bernard Kouchner?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the French minister of culture, as far as I recall, an idealist who came down to help. I don't know why and how, but he came. I have only passed him en route to -- when he was going south and we were going north from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the letter it says, in the second sentence: "I have told you that your negotiating partner on the JNA side, Colonel Svicevic is not an acceptable partner for negotiations in which ECMM monitors are engaged, even as an eye witness. Colonel -- I'm sorry, Mr. Svicevic has threatened to kill more than one team of monitors and this with so much conviction that some monitors have since decided to leave Yugoslavia." Were you aware of that situation with Colonel Svicevic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have met the monitors who report this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only tell that when these people came back from meeting this man, he actively threatened their lives. He said, I want to kill you -- even said, I will kill you. So that's the sense of it. I cannot quote the exact wording, but that -- the sort of words they brought back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2, there's a 1 and a 2, it says: "Negotiations on your level should not be with a mere colonel, but with the commander in charge, General Strugar." What's your view on that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
