utterances.text: Well, I agree with Ambassador Van Houten, because I think when you discuss -- started discussing with the minister, it would be appropriate that he was dealing with the highest-ranking and the commanding officer in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this letter was written by Mr. Van Houten?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was your eventual supervisor or boss?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the EC monitor mission in Zagreb; that means he was in my language the commander of all the EC monitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look at the next tab, tab Number 26, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that letter before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that letter to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's to the head of mission; that means, again, Ambassador Van Houten in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's from?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Minister Kouch -- Kouchner, my French is not that good. Kouchner I think he was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is this letter about, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he is telling about that he has now started discussing the situation with both parties and that he has changed from -- so it's the situation in Dubrovnik that we are talking about, that he has changed partners, so he's not talking to this colonel mentioned before but to a general now and to Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No it says on that line right there that you just mentioned: "Negotiations are now on the federal side at the level of General Damjanovic and Admiral Jokic."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was apparently the sort of the good advice he got from Mr. Van Houten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever dealt with this Damjanovic Mr. Damjanovic, or General Damjanovic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes -- unless there are two of the name. Because when the colonel I dealt with in Zelenika who was called or named as the second in command in General Strugar's outfit, he had the same name but he was a colonel at the time, to the best of my knowledge. So if there are two, I wouldn't know. It's the same name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move on to Document 27, please. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it before, a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the third full paragraph which begins: "During the meeting, the Croatian side," the last sentence says: "Either a separate agreement is reached, which in essence will give Dubrovnik a status apart or hostilities will resume and justify the fair accompli of a breech of cease-fire and further destruction of the ancient city." Did you agree, based on the circumstances which existed in this state on the 24th of November, that without any cease-fire agreement, the Old Town of Dubrovnik would be in danger, based on your knowledge of what was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I had seen and according to all the reports I had got, yes, I found there was a great danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would you say that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the shelling of the town up until the time, and not only the town, but hotels with refugees and, et cetera, civilians in general, you know, you could be very doubtful if somebody wanted to be more kind to that town. I -- the situation was not pleasant by any chance, and I think it could -- I had a feeling at the time, from what I had seen, what I could see was happening, that there was a danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the last document for November, which is tab number 28.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a memorandum of agreement, as the heading says, made in Dubrovnik apparently. I was not present, but that is what it says and I have seen it before, where you had a meeting apparently with this General Damjanovic, Admiral Jokic, and the mayor of Dubrovnik, and Mr. Kouchner. What is important to me about this document is that it is stated here that people who threaten monitors are not suitable partners in negotiations and should be excluded from all negotiations while monitors are present. Well, that was necessary. We were threatened and I was threatened myself in Zelenika before when we were down there. And written guarantees concerning the Churchill [phoen] monitors from both parties should be given beforehand by parties involved and local commanders and authorities. Under no circumstances are they or the locations where they are staying or operating to be fired upon or otherwise threatened. Well, this was signed by two officers, senior officers, from the JNA on -- and in the French minister's presence and the mayor of Dubrovnik's presence on the 25th of November. I wanted this time as a witness to state that this was nothing, absolutely nothing worth, because on the 6th of December the JNA were shelling the place where they knew we were, some monitors, and free Croatian ministers. We had taken part in the meeting in Cavtat on the 5th. On the 6th they were shelling us. They knew we were there because we were going to have a meeting again on the 6th, and they were shelling us again. We had the meeting on the 7th. So this they signed is nothing worth, not the paper it is written on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the agreement was not abided by?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this applied to lots of other things. You might have noted earlier that there was a note that this was the 13th cease-fire agreement. I think that was a letter from Mr. Van Houten mentioned that the 13th -- this was incredible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a meeting on December 5th. Why don't we move to tab Number 29 which concerns that meeting. Just look at it first, and then I'll ask you some questions about the meeting after we look at it.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, first, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us -- you don't have to read it from memory, what happened on December 5th? Tell us about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope you appreciate my handwriting this time. Well, the meeting came into being because a couple of days earlier I was contacted by Minister Rudolf whom I had taken -- well, had taken part in negotiations a number of times before in Split with General Mladenic and other persons. He wanted us or he wanted me to go down with him because he said he had arranged through his means a meeting in Cavtat with the JNA. And it was obvious that when he put in a request like that and had it arranged, that of course I should go because that was why we were there, we were, let's say, the monitors were there as sort of mid-wives, if possible, at the -- any discussions taking part between the two parties. And general -- so the philosophy of the mission was so that they should try to negotiate between themselves and we were there to try to make the situation calm and that we were not starting every situation -- discussion from the Ottomans Empire's time and what have you. So that was why he asked me. So, I said Yes, and then of course I needed an interpreter, so I had an interpreter. And then I knew from previous experience it's nice to have another colleague, so I took one of my trusted staff officers along. And we said yes and then showed up. There was three ministers going. So we went down first on the 4th of December to Dubrovnik. It was reasonably peaceful. There was only one rifle shot coming through the restaurant window while we had dinner. But, we went down to Cavtat, as arranged, the next day. And then we were requested by the JNA, we were met by Admiral Jokic and my friend Captain Jeremic. And they asked that we should not be present at the meeting. And the Croatian ministers accepted that, so we enjoyed the beauty of the nature outside. After the meeting, the ministers and Admiral Jokic came out. And we were informed that they had not completed -- had not ended up with a final result, but the Minister Rudolf informed clearly that the meeting had taken place in a good and friendly, positive, atmosphere. Now, that was the word, so that could only indicate that everything was all right. Nothing, as I mentioned here, had been written down, but they were going to resume the meeting the next day and hopefully -- and they were absolutely convinced, the three ministers, they pressed that clearly, that they would end up with a result. And as you can see it's listed there, the meeting was to take place on the 6th in the morning, at 1000 hours in Cavtat again. Again this was typical to me that it always had to be on the JNA territory. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you a question. What was the feelings of the parties. Was it -- after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say again that the ministers expressed optimism and hope. Admiral Jokic was smiling and friendly. And so according to the clear information, the way people behaved, it seemed like the situation was positive and there was hope for a good result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you anticipate an agreement on the following day?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you anticipate it, not what happened on the following day, based on the positive --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I felt like that. And when we returned to Dubrovnik and we had completed our fancy reports and what have you informing our superiors and our headquarters, we were having dinner, not sitting at the same table, but the EC monitors I had along with and I had a pleasant evening -- we were helpful, and it seemed like the Croatian ministers and people from the crisis committee or whoever from the Croat side who were also there were in a good mood and helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you brought the Croatian -- you escorted the Croatian ministers there. Who did you expect to be there from the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had expected that it would be the commander. I had expected it would be Admiral Strugar, but it was Admiral Jokic -- sorry, General Strugar. It was Admiral Jokic that was there. And so I assumed that he was the representative of General Strugar; however, I was not the man who was -- had asked for and was taking part in the discussions. And I can admit that I don't know if Mr. Rudolf actually -- what he expected. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, based on your own anticipation of an agreement on the following day and the fact that everyone was so positive on December 5th, did you expect shelling on December 7th -- I'm sorry, December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No chance. Actually, I went to bed and read a book and I was quite happy. You say, well, there's hope now. I had no idea what -- I knew I had to be down for that meeting the next day. And I was prepared for work. That was it. I had no thought whatsoever of when you -- sending and accepting -- three ministers from Croatia accepting to have a meeting, starting the meeting the day before, that it was not going to continue. To meet with -- meet with -- I didn't have a thought. And when the whole situation changed, I was really, honestly, very, very surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned three ministers from Croatia. The fact that ministers had taken part in this meeting as opposed to Crisis Staff members, the local civilian officials in the past, did that have any significance for you?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it indicated to me that now we were working on a high level, so it was very important from -- anyway, from the Croatian side. It was something which was now a very serious and important matter to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to December 6th. Can you first tell us where you were on the -- in the early morning of December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my bed, in my room, facing the sea, with a bathtub full of salty water for drinking and brushing teeth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in -- could you tell us where, which hotel, or which house or room?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hotel was Hotel Argentina. Room number, I cannot remember. I did not keep the receipt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. Did you -- why did you stay in Dubrovnik that night? You didn't go back to Split?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be a bit like going to Oslo to have a meeting in London the next day or something like that. We were down there. We -- you could take a whole day to go back to Split. And when you're having a meeting, you're finishing off in the afternoon in the 5th, having a meeting at 10.00 in the morning on the 6th, it was obvious we had to stay in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were there for negotiations on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there ready for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And were you to accompany the three Croatian ministers?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were going to have exactly the same setup as we had on the 5th. We were three monitors going down with three ministers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did something happen in the early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I woke up because of certain noise which was -- is a bit too familiar for me. But I woke up because I could hear impact shelling and what have you, just about -- before 6.00. And I got organised. And as you can imagine at the time, there were not that many guests at Hotel Argentina. There were lots of refugees in other hotels, but not here. So I had to find people. You had people coming out and shaking their heads. And then I could -- before I actually went down, I could see out of the window from my hotel room, when I pulled the curtain away, I could see wire-guiding missiles going towards the Old City walls, Argosy -- yeah, Argosy Harbour, it's called, the old harbour in Dubrovnik. So then we got -- tried to get down, get communication, and find out what was going on. And as soon as I had possibilities, I sent a complaint down for those we had now been negotiating with Admiral Jokic the day before. As far as I recall I sent -- addressed the message to him, complained about the shelling of Dubrovnik, which from that time on was increasing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- we'll get to that in a second. But prior to that shelling which woke you up around 6.00 a.m., did you hear any other gunfire prior to that, anywhere from 2.00 a.m. to -- to that time when you first heard the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. And my two colleagues did not. And I heard of nobody who had heard anything before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that initial shelling that you heard at 6.00 a.m., did you receive any protests or did the ECMM monitors receive any protests of any military action, breaking the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By any party? Did anyone notify the ECMM prior to hearing the shelling of any cease-fire violation or any military action of any kind?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you maintain a log of the day's events of December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to turn to tab 30, please. Could you look at that document and tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is my log sheet. To be honest, I had not expected I had to use paper on that sort of stuff, but this is -- I started immediately, and I can see -- shelling from land and sea, the first mark 0600 hours. It started a bit before 6.00, but I'm not going to give you the exact minute of the time, but it was for sure in progress at 6.00 in the morning. And as you can see, of course, I reported immediately to Split and Zagreb by the means I had available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based on your observations, two impacts hit the old centre at about 7.20?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw them myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then over the next 12 minutes there were numerous impacts into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the last line, 9.45 to 10.00, you have: "Between 10 and 15 heavy explosions per minute."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you time these or what do you do?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had various things to do down in the basement of the Hotel Argentina. And these are -- at the time, well, of course, I could hear the noise all the time, but I was also taking -- getting information from my two colleagues, whereas we always at least had one out observing what was going on. So this is a report of observation coming from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at 9.20, let's move up a couple. "Our boat," it looks like something Cavtat, or at Cavtat, "for Cavtat, Argus 2, mounted with the EC flag hit directly and inflames along with Argus 1." Could you tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a very precise hit, I must say, very efficient, no boat, lots of smoke. There was a huge EC flag, a huge big one with a circle of yellow stars. It was a wonderful target, very good for an artillery observer to look at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been using that boat?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the boat we were sailing down to Cavtat with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2, if we could. At 11.00 it says: "Frequency," -- I'm sorry, 10.45 to 11.00, "Frequency is now 15 heavy shells per minute with some minutes' interval."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's not much more to tell. That was what was a fact and what, as I say -- some of it I might have been out looking and I was out looking, yes. And one of my colleagues or maybe both of them were observing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at 11.10 it says: "Minister Rudolf talking to Zagreb. Message from Boka Kotorska Naval Base. JNA will cease fire at 1115 hours. A meeting in Cavtat is planned for 1330 hours," and something after that.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Inch Alla" is Arabic and means "God willing".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: God willing. Okay. Where was Minister Rudolf at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the same basement, or most of the time in the same room as I was at the bottom of Hotel Argentina. And actually, the message is from Boka Kotorska as far as I know. It's called the naval base that -- well, he has on his means, he was operating on another phone. Now and then we were operating on the same. We had problems with the communication, but he apparently had had this contact and managed to get hold of Zagreb through some telephone line. That's what it is about. And I'm sorry about my remark, but anyway it's a good remark, God willing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the firing stop at 11.15?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. As you can see, you have a few minutes later. Frequency dropped considerably, that means they were still firing but not with the same intensity as before. There might have been a stop exactly at 11.15, but it certainly was resumed immediately after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you go to the next page to 1430 hours, which is 2.30, 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "Minister Rudolf receives message from Admiral Jokic who apologises for the shelling and informs that it is out of JNA control. Shelling sporadic. Still in progress. Jokic informs that he had to be in Belgrade at 1400 hours. Admiral Jokic suggests a meeting tomorrow at 12.00." Now -- actually, after it says shelling is out of JNA control, you wrote "unbelievable." Could you tell us what that is all about.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. We actually -- I also received a copy of a message from Admiral Jokic, who apologised -- I think there might be a copy around, anyway I had a copy of it -- where he apologies for what happened or what had happened during that day until now. And my remark "unbelievable" a soldier's remark, because it was my opinion that the Yugoslav army was a professional, well-organised army. And to me, in an area like that it sounds unbelievable that you can go on with a shelling for so long because something is out of hand. It seemed to me that they, between themselves, had good communication. I could understand if a single rifle man in the first line had not got a message or got scared of something, and a single rifle shot can now and then start a war -- a minor war in the area. But this was a constant ongoing fire by heavy weapons. And that it -- you can use the remark "something got out of hand," it -- so it's really unbelievable that a high-ranking officer could say so or write so. I never expected, of course, that this was -- this was a private note, let's say, to my headquarters, but I really felt it was unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue on the next page. By the way, did shelling stop at that point?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- sorry, are you saying next page now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, next page. 1610, which is 4.10 p.m. "Only a few impacts since 1600 hours. Minister Rudolf informs me that General Strugar has now ordered immediate CF," - cease-fire - "however the" --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Odd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Odd grenade still arrives." Could you tell me about that, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through his means, Minister Rudolf got in contact with the JNA. And according to the information he gave with General Strugar. So the general was back in the area on the scene somehow. And so it was a promise, again of a cease-fire. And I can easily understand, reference to what I said before, that that might be difficult that it just ends at that specific time. So I was not too surprised if the cease-fire was really ordered, that the odd grenade still arrived in our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there much shelling after General Strugar ordered a cease-fire at 4.15 or 1615?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not much, so it appeared everything was in hand more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have been 1610 or 1600. What time did all shelling, even the sporadic shelling, finally end, according to your notes?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was -- the absolute last part of the show was for sure at 1915, but it was not much. It was like Christmas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move to a set of three documents relating to December 6th, Documents 31, 32, and 34. Let us start with Document 31. The English part is from the middle to the bottom. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it myself. I got somebody to type it for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, I have in my handwriting noted that it was passed on by the means I had, fax I think, at the time, at 06, that means the 6th of December, at 7.14. The whole thing when I got out of bed at 06.00. Well, it took a bit of time to get things organised and working, communications through, et cetera. So it was -- the best thing I could do was immediately -- as fast as I could to protest against this thing, starting at the very same morning as we were going to have a meeting. And as apparently the person in charge of the meeting were two -- three ministers, was Admiral Jokic, and he was the person we were going to meet again that day, I found that it was relevant to send this message to him, and he was the addressee then. And the message itself I think talks for itself -- I hope so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that "the attack on Dubrovnik stands in complete opposition to the good will you expressed yesterday." Is that a reference to the positive feelings after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, for the Court, Your Honour, on Sunday the witness brought a small piece of paper with him which is barely legible, and it is like a fax transmission notice of a fax machine. You need a magnifying glass to read it, but it does indicate that it was sent. Would the Court like this? We've tried to make a copy; it can't be read. But he does have this in his notes. Would the Court like to examine it? He has it in his personal notes. If the Court would like to examine it, or the counsel, or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, if Defence counsel could see it and then pass it to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have that small sheet of paper that's the ...

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about this lousy copy?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This. I've got that, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just checking something. Because I was using a magnifying glass to try to read this again. And I'm just checking if I actually have got that. Anyway, this is the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's on the small strip of paper. It's hard to read, but it can be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Weiner, that Mr. Hvalkof has been able to read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's legible. It can be read. It indicates that it was sent at 7.12 a.m., and I just wanted the Court to know it's a -- it comes off of the fax machine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a fax transmission --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this, as far as I can see, is a confirmation. The time is 1535 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're not receiving any translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a confirmation with this fax, and the time is 1535. If I look at the content, I don't think this is the same fax that my learned friend and colleague has spoken about. It may be an error. Perhaps a different document has been given instead of the one that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the wrong one. I'm sorry. Thank you. Wait a minute. I'm sorry about all these old papers. I've got the right one. I do apologise for the mess in my papers. Here you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this reaches you, I can tell you what we are able to see on this slip of paper. It says the 6th of December up there, 12 minutes past 7.00. That's what it says. That's when it was sent, apparently. But what is noteworthy about this document is that the section which refers to remote ID, or rather, where the recipient should be, this portion is the portion missing. It has been torn off apparently, so we can't see who received this fax. You will see this in a short while. You can see parts of the numbers 8 and 5, but you can't see the entire number, really. So this bit is missing, and you can have a look for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that help, Mr. Petrovic. Are you wanting the document back, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It was the witness's document. I was just going to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can I see it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be helpful if all numerals and words which the witness can identify are recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me read it into the record, and then I'll hand it to him. It says: "Report, December 06, 1991, 07:12," and then under it has certain words: "Mode, duration, page, result." Under duration it has five something, appears to be minutes. And then it says: "Transmit," it looks like G3, N something. And on the left it says: "December 6th -- or December 06, 07." It has a date. A start time which just has a 707, and you can't see the rest, for the record. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it you agree with the observation of Mr. Petrovic that the number of the recipient cannot be identified?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. That's why the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what happened to the rest of that sheet of paper, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. It's a -- at the time it was of no importance. When I got this piece from the fellow who was sending the fax message, it was just to prove to me, because normally when you get a fax message, then it was proved to me that it was sent. And you get an information to say okay or whatever that the line was sent. And it was sent on a fax machine from the basement of the Hotel Argentina, and by one of my colleagues. And I said, Well, just put this on a -- because that was sort of my confirmation and then I noted down. It has been sent. So I was absolutely sure at the time - sorry - that it had been received by Admiral Jokic or his headquarters, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that little strip of confirmation sheet stapled to another document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever -- when I did this sort of thing, sit in a situation like this, I had a staple machine, I would do it this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document which it's stapled to, which is your personal document, is that the same document as tab Number 31?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And on your original -- on your tab 31 it says to the right of your name, on the English, on the bottom, could you read that and explain.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sent 0607, 14, alpha November 1991." That means sent at the 6th of November, which is wrong. It should, of course, be December. I was old and tired on the day. Sent on the 6th of December on 7.14, so -- 1991. And as you can see up at the top, it is Dubrovnik, December 6th, 1991. So it's just because I had been busy, I made the same mistake as Mr. Bondioli as the previous mentioned document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us, Mr. Hvalkof -- I'm sorry, are you able to assist us, Mr. Hvalkof, with the -- how you sent it, to what number was it transmitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot assist you with the number, Your Honour. I can only -- I only know -- the number is out. But it was sent to the fax number with the JNA down in whatever, Zelenika, Boka, wherever it was. I don't know where the place was, but we had a fax number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, it is obvious that the original of this document is still with the witness, the one that we had been looking at. However, at tab 31 the document is there. But unlike all the other faxes under this tab, there is no photocopy at the top of the page of this small slip of paper that we looked at a while ago. The issue of the authenticity of this document requires further clarification as to why, if this indeed is a document, the original of which the witness is in possession of, why is this bit missing then? Perhaps we can clarify this on cross-examination, or perhaps we can receive an answer now, especially in the light of the fact that at tab 30 on page 1, there is no indication whatsoever that this witness ever sent this document to begin with. If you look at tab 30, there's nothing about it there. 7.00, 10 past 7.00, quarter past 7.00, some of his other activities were written down at the time, but there's nothing about this. This is the only thing I wish to draw your attention to for the time being, and we will continue to probe this matter on cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, they certainly are issues you would want to pursue in cross-examination, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the other thing, Your Honour, I've tried several times to photocopy that. If the Registry has any access to anything, either photocopying or any special machine that could photocopy that, we would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears from my relatively unskilled eye to be unable to be reduced satisfactorily by photocopy. It would require ordinary photography, I think, to have any prospect of producing some sort of legible result. I take it you are wishing to tender the original, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I left it in the hands of the witness; it's his document. We have a copy. Would you mind --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Be my guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What you have passed to the Court, Mr. Hvalkof, you say is the original of the document at tab 31. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With the transmission slip stapled to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that form, it will be received as a separate document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P62.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Hvalkof. Now, let's move to the next document also dated December 6th, tab number 32. And the second page is typed; it's a little bit more legible. Could you tell us about this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a complaint to the JNA at Boka from the crisis committee, and it's sent as an info, information message, to us, the ECMM people, at that time in Dubrovnik. So it is again a protest of the same nature as mine about the shelling. And I don't think there is much more to say about it, that they just informed us that they had sent this through their means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is also dated December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then another document, Document 34.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us how you came about this document.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was also passed on to us as an info. I cannot tell you exactly who gave it to us, but it was passed to us down there in Dubrovnik. It is again an info message by this information centre of Dubrovnik. I have previously stated that I am not fully aware of the -- actually, the various parts of the Dubrovnik administration organisation, but this information centre was no doubt or was connected with the crisis committee and the town council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this letter, it also, or this fax or information sheet, let's call it a document, it also discusses the damage in the Old Town at both 10.00 as well as 1445, which is 2.45 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, the first thing here they said -- well, this is how they saw it, their version of what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you received and maintained documents from various sources?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we move to a set of letters, 35, 36, and 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Weiner, it might be convenient to break now before you go into that group of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hvalkof. Before we left, I asked you to look at a group of three documents, tabs 35, 36, and 33. Let's start with tab 35. Do you know who sent this?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a message from JNA headquarters in Boka sent to Minister Rudolf by Vice-Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's a letter of apology, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the letter in the first paragraph it says that General Kadijevic has sent a message to you and the ECMM in Dubrovnik on undertaking an energetic investigation on our responsibility and the guilt -- the guilty ones for this event. Were you ever aware of any investigation that was undertaken?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone from --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except, sorry, except for the information here, but I have not received anything of this nature myself addressed to me as an ECM member in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was anyone from your staff or any ECMM monitors ever questioned by members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To an investigation on what happened on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to an investigation. The only thing I remember in that connection was that it was arranged that two JNA officers were coming to make an inspection and having a trip for sight seeing of the beauties of Dubrovnik after the whole story. But I had -- I was -- I know nothing else about this investigation, that what is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than that inspection of Dubrovnik, and we'll get to that shortly, did anyone ever question or ask to interview either yourself or and members of your monitoring staff concerning the incident of December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are meaning the JNA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever advised of the results of the energetic investigation, as described by General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that much later. I had a copy I believe from our headquarters in Zagreb. That I can't remember. But I can remember that I read a paper where they were listing all the damages they saw or the way they saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn of anyone being punished?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to tab number 36. Now, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is it from?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from Colonel General Pavle Strugar to Minister Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does General Strugar indicate in his letter -- actually, could you read it?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well: "This morning JNA, Yugoslav People's Army forces were fired upon with mortars and machine guns from S-r-d" - Srdj, I think it's pronounced - "and Babin Kuk without provocation, our forces returned fire in response to this action; however, on my orders, the units ceased fire at 1115 hours, though your forces did not respect the cease-fire. And it can therefore be concluded that the buildings in the old heart of Dubrovnik are being damaged by the fire your forces are laying down."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction to General Strugar's letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised because I received that later than I had received previous apology we had just talked about by Admiral Jokic. I was also surprised in the way that the -- to the best of what I observed, fire didn't cease at the time mentioned here, 1115 hours. It ceased much later, finally, after 1800 hours in the evening. 1915 I think was the last time we noted something or when I was sure nothing was happening. And to me it is double Dutch or Chinese the last part of it that this could then be concluded that the Croats were shelling themselves. I just don't understand it, and I didn't understand it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that letter, just back to the middle part of the letter, General Strugar states: "On my orders, the units ceased fire on 1115 hours." If you go back to Exhibit 30, just for one moment back to Exhibit 30, to the second page. Does not that correspond to 1110, Minister Rudolf talking to Zagreb message, JNA will cease fire at 1115 hours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other comments on this letter from General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comments?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, any others?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, prior to this statement in General Strugar's letter that the JNA forces were fired on, had you received any communication from the JNA indicating that from midnight until 6.00 a.m when -- approximately 6.00 a.m. when you were awoken -- awaken, that there was any fire in violation of the cease-fire from the JNA or from any party?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I didn't hear anything myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now move on to Exhibit Number 33, just back a few. Now, could you tell us about this fax, sir. When I say "Exhibit 33," tab 33. Could you tell us about this letter or fax.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure what you want me to tell you, but it is a letter from -- to General Pavle Strugar from Minister Davorin Rudolf concerning the situation in Dubrovnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the letter it says that Minister Rudolf -- in the letter Minister Rudolf invites General Strugar to visit the Old Town and see the damage. Do you know whether General Strugar did, in fact, visit the town and observe the damage?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general did not visit the town when I was there. I didn't see him anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- and did you maintain this letter in your ECMM records?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we were given copies, as I mentioned before, down there. Whatever information the Croats were sending out or receiving, they also informed us about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could we now move to tab 37, please. Could you tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is again one of my log sheets. And that is from the 7th of December, 1991, referring to what happened -- what we did that day. And it's sent as -- whenever I had a chance, it was sent on fax to a headquarters -- our regional headquarters in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mine, one of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there's an indication of a visit to the Old Town at 9.15. Did you visit the Old Town on that day?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The monitors and I walked around, as far as I know, along with the crisis committee and the ministers to have an idea of what had happened to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you said you were with monitors, who were you with on that date?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was with Hans van Beek, and a Dutchman and a Dane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When had you previously visited the Old Town prior to December 7th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th and also on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Old Town look the same as it had looked on December 5th or December 4th and 5th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the difference?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had burning houses, ruined houses, impacts -- shelling impacts of -- shells all over the place. It looks like a missile garbage lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you visited on the 5th, do you recall who you were with from your team?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was along on the 5th with my two colleagues and a part of it was a member of the crisis committee. But in general, we walked around by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said previously when you went to the meeting on the 5th, you were with a trusted colleague or a trusted associate or associates. Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the early -- on the 5th, when you went to the meeting on the 5th, you said you brought a trusted associate and that's before you walked [phoen] him.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was again Hans van Beek and Lars Brolund.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us how long had you worked with Lars Brolund?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I came to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he, could you tell us, on December 6th while the shelling was going on.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- he was with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he act during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us your opinion as to his effectiveness as a monitor or employee?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a good monitor. He was efficient and very nice to deal with, professional, with a good sense of humour, which is very important in cases like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was he -- he was also with you on this walk around of the Old Town on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the walk around or the inspection or the observation of the Old Town, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the walk about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to this hospital to look at wounded people and dead bodies and that sort of stuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the afternoon, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had at that time arranged for a new meeting in Cavtat, or we had, again that was minister Rudolf and we and his people. So there was arranged a meeting so -- in Cavtat -- well, actually that was the meeting that was supposed to have taken place the day before. So we went down there again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you see at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic and Captain Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any conversation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were met in a decent and proper way. And then immediately after we met on a boat in the harbour, and there was -- then the discussions started again with the ministers and the Admiral Jokic and his -- Captain Jeremic. There might have been another from the JNA. I cannot remember that. It started on the boat. But what was remarkable is the day before, or two days before, the JNA did not want our presence. There was nothing of that nature this time. We were present all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you offer any suggestions to the negotiation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I remember I offered some suggestions very -- you know, as I have said before, we were sort of there trying to help the negotiations just to move on in a decent way. But we could add -- give remarks, of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. course if you wanted to or if we were asked to. So yes, I did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we move to the next document, number 38. Now, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 38 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 38, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an agreement reached during that meeting on December 7th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the agreement. It was all made except for my remark -- it was all made by the two involved parties. They were talking in decent language and the atmosphere was, I would say, pretty good when you had in mind what had happened the day before. The behaved like gentlemen and fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present for the signatures?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there the whole time. And I was signing the agreement myself as a witness, you could say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the third page there's an Article 9. "The implementation of this agreement will be monitored by the ECMM. To the ECMM, both sides guarantee insights in all situations, including their personal security and movement in the whole area." Who suggested that that article be included in this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew and I know that Minister Rudolf was mentioning it, but I also know that I had given remarks in connection with the talks that that was essential, as I have said before, if anything like that has to work, you must have neutral people on both sides. And I had put in remarks in that connection at the end of these talks, before this document was actually written in an office in the harbour area, wherever. So that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go to the next document, document 39. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the walk through or notes about the walk through that you discussed with the JNA inspectors?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be, because I mentioned before I saw this document quite some time later. It's -- I can't say, but I certainly didn't see it before -- maybe in the middle of December or something. It was much later I saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who signed the, and who was it sent to. Who's it from?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from Vice-Admiral Jokic -- actually, I don't know how and where it was sent to. And anyway, I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this document it describes certain damage in the Old Town. Do you agree with this characterisation of the damage to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Anyway, it may be a matter of understanding of words. And my understanding, if you look at the para 1 saying there were visible traces of damage on some houses caused by small-calibre shells. My translation of what I saw would not be small-calibre shells; it would be heavier shells, heavier weapons. I don't deny that there might have been small-calibre shells as well, but in general the damage was made by more severe weapons. And it also looked very much like that when the impacts came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any other disagreements with the characterisation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the words like "slight," and that sort of thing, of course there were places where there was slight damage. In general, the town of Dubrovnik looked very horrible and very badly damaged. I think this is a very, very, very mild interpretation of the facts of life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we move to the next tab, number 40, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've seen this before, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are just notes. I cannot tell you who they are made by, but of course when you had moved out to a place, an area, you needed to know who you were dealing with. So we would also -- a monitor would always take notes, try to find out, who am I dealing with, and note it down so you knew the names, also a question of decent politeness when you met people, you knew who you were dealing with and writing to, et cetera. So this is -- I've seen the same names listed up in, let's say, a more official way in Split, for example. So here you have a list of the people you're dealing with on the JNA side and a list of people you are dealing with on the crisis committee. And this is absolutely quite normal. You took those type of notes down whenever you started business somewhere. You wanted to know, who am I dealing with?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the JNA offices. Who had you dealt with or had you had communication with on the JNA side, the top part of the ladder?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it states: First, General Strugar, Admiral Jokic, liaison officer, as we called him, Jeremic, we talked about him before. And then the interpreter, I can't remember, I never met that man. And then the political officer I -- it's apparently the one -- I'm not too sure if that is the one that was referred to earlier as the one the head of mission didn't want us to talk to. But anyway they are -- I haven't met the last people. I met the three first. And the other ones in general, I met them in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "the other ones," are you referring to the crisis committee?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis committee, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the president of the crisis commit you met with a Mr. Sikic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this doctor, Poljanic.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The mayor? What about the deputy mayor?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now did you actually meet Admiral Strugar or just correspond -- speak to him by telephone?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never had the honour of meeting General Strugar before in this room, if that is meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we move to document 41. We're on the last two -- actually, if you go to the second page, it's in B/C/S but the names are legible. It's easier to read. Have you ever seen this type of chart before at ECMM meetings?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this particular one, but when you found out what an organisation was about, you would make something similar, because it's a quite typical military way of doing it. I have not seen this one before, as I recall. But this is a typical thing to make. I do not know who made it -- well, probably it's maybe listed at the back, but I'm not familiar as such with this. And I have not seen it this particular one while I was in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who in ECMM made these types of charts?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you do -- that would be in the operational staff normally as you do it. So that would be one of the operations officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where are the operations officers in ECMM get the information to produce these types of charts?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know but -- where this is coming from. But for example, if you go down to Dubrovnik and you try to start up a mission there and try to work, you try to find out who are you dealing with. So you get the names of these people. And for example, the list we showed before, then you had the names of the JNA part. So then you would find some officers and -- not all people in the mission were officers, go back and say, now we know that they inform us that this man is the commander-in-chief here, this is his deputy, this is his ADC, or whatever. It would be normal for most officers to go down and try and say, can you make it like this, this type of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based on the information you had -- or actually, this chart places General Strugar at the top of a hierarchy. Based on the information you had, who was the commander of the JNA forces in the area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the best of my knowledge all the time, it was General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This chart indicates a General Damjanovic on the second level. What was the name of the person that you were told was the second in command or his deputy?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was in Zelenika the first time, I was informed that that was -- when he showed up, I was informed in advance that that would be Colonel Damjanovic who came, that would be wrong, but then that was only way the person apparently - that's what he said he was called - when he showed up. And I have -- the only information I have or I had at that time personally was what I got from the JNA, that it was General Strugar's second in command who was showing up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we go to the last document, tab number 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we discuss this, I just want to note for the record, this is an article that was in Danish. It was sent out to be translated. Somehow a page was not translated. The witness has agreed to send us another copy of the article. I've talked to the Defence. They have no objection to having it admitted and as soon as we receive the newly-translated article, we would just replace it with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what that document is, sir.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I come from a -- graduated from the oldest boarding school back home. And we -- every month we received a very nice -- what would you call, monthly, weekly. And then the editor asked me, as an old student from that school, to write about the experience. And I said, Yes, well, okay. I'll do so. So it was put up in two articles. I tried to describe my experience in ex-Yugoslavia. At the time -- as I saw it and from my notes. It was split up in two articles. The first two pages are from the first and then there was something. So they wanted the rest to come the next volume. And then they somehow, when I handed this over to the investigators who were visiting me on the 6th, 7th, 8th, April, 2002, the second page looked very much -- my nasty photo was on that one, too. So they must have thought the same, as their Danish was not very good. So they were probably only taking a copy of one page because my picture was on the -- forgotten the second -- the start of the second article, second part of the article, as it was split-up by the editor. I am -- the way -- what I had written was the way I saw it, the way I believe it was, the way felt it was, and my opinion about the -- my experience down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "down there," you mean the area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean in the whole ECMM mission, because I'm starting telling about evacuation of Borongaj barracks in Zagreb and on the trip down and what have you. But the main part of it concerns my experience in Split area and Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to ask you some general questions to finish off here. On December 6th, did you witness any outgoing fire from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the monitors witness or notify you that they witnessed any outgoing fire from the Old Town on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either you or any of the monitors observe any outgoing fire at any time in October, November, or December from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a tough question because mentioning pretty much. And I am sure that there must have been some outgoing, but that in general would have been small-arms fire. There was a war going on and of course the Croats had been shooting. But if you ask me now, I have no exact information about it, of course there has been firing. But not -- I have not observed it myself during my stay down there and my two colleagues have not observed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you ever seen any monitoring reports where anyone, any monitor, had observed outgoing fire from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, had you or any of your colleagues ever observed any mortars in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Old Town suitable for mortars?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a mortar needs to be placed on earth, not too soft ground, too much, but it sort of -- is constructed so it has to -- when you fire the first shot is never going to be very good. But the first -- then the mortar settles in the ground. And then you can start doing your proper job. But if you make a visit to Dubrovnik, there's not very many places in the Old City to place a mortar. It would be jumping around more dangerous to yourself than anybody else. But I -- anyway, I have no reports from any of my people and I have not seen anything like that in the town. I can add that mortars are a different option. You might have tiny, small 60-millimetre ones which are -- only more or less as useful as a hand grenade. So there would be another [indiscernible] to anybody outside the town. You have 81 or 80, those different calibers around 80-millimetre mortars which can jump along, but they were not there. We have not seen them. And you have 120-millimetre or even bigger mortars, and that -- not -- in my opinion not very suitable. I would not use in general a mortar from that area, and I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of any artillery --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Being placed in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had any of the ECMM monitors ever noted any artillery?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody reported that to me while I was there. They would have done if they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's my -- that would have been my next question. If an ECMM monitor, one of your monitors which you supervised, had observed something like that, would that have been a matter for reporting up the line?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we tried to keep control of what was happening and we are trying to be neutral people. So it is important -- so what we know what people are dealing with. And in case something happens that you sort of confirm, these people had actually these weapons and be able to sort of find out if they're using them. It's a normal part of being a neutral man observing a cease-fire, just a routine job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally: Did you see any sort of military constructions, if you want to call them, in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would include trenches, bunkers, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. It would be very difficult to dig a trench in there, but no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally: Any sign, did you or your monitors see any sign of any heavy weaponry in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the Prosecution's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the time and since our examination-in-chief [as interpreted] is likely to be quite comprehensive, as was that by my colleague, I am not sure it's a good idea to start now with only 15 minutes to go, or perhaps we should start tomorrow to get more continuity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We think that may be a practical proposal, in view of the extent and nature of the evidence which you are to deal with. So we will adjourn now until tomorrow, Mr. Rodic, to enable you to better prepare --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... For what you want to deal with. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection to closing earlier. But just one housekeeping matter. Counsel has requested copies of the Kaiser [phoen] exhibits and we will produce them as soon as we finish here, as soon as we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Hvalkof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My horses and dogs are waiting for me. When can I go back home?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would like to be able to give you an answer, Mr. Hvalkof. Perhaps Mr. Rodic can offer some assistance. How long do you expect to be, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's very difficult to say at this point with any degree of precision whatsoever, but I do have a rough idea. It will take the whole day today [as interpretd] to complete my cross-examination, in view of the number of documents that have been introduced, in view of the importance of this witness for our case. Of course my learned friend from the OTP went through the documents as he saw fit, but we for our part must work through these documents in quite some detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that's the case, Mr. Rodic, I think it ambitious of you to suggest that you would finish in one day. Am I being too pessimistic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will certainly do my best, that's what I can say for sure. I will certainly be using up the whole day tomorrow, but I really can't say whether I will be able to complete my cross-examination tomorrow or not. Perhaps I will need some more time, briefly I hope, on the day after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will live in hope that your first expression proves to be correct, Mr. Rodic. Well, you've heard all of that, Mr. Hvalkof. I wouldn't make a booking tomorrow evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm anyway not doing that, Your Honours. Your organisation is doing it. It's not the first time I've been detained like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I hope your animals can wait in patience. We will adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: at 1.33 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
